newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn plays down nuclear element in French dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Bonn plays down nuclear element in French dialogue.

text.p: Germany welcomed France's offer to hold a dialogue on future defence cooperation but played down the mention of nuclear weapons in a document, saying on Tuesday it did not alter Bonn's post-war renunciation of atomic weapons.

The government's chief spokesman Peter Hausmann and his counterparts in the Defence and Foreign Ministries said the agreement was just a small part of a joint document mapping out future defence policy cooperation between Germany and France.

"This is an an offer of dialogue which has been made and which the German government is accepting. It changes nothing on the principles of our policy," Hausmann told the regular post-cabinet news conference given by government spokesmen.
"Germany last renounced the production, possession and control of nuclear weapons in the 1990 Two-Plus-Four Treaty. Nothing has changed in that," Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann added.
The document was agreed at a Franco-German summit last month but only became public when the French newspaper Le Monde published extracts of the text last week.

A senior government official welcomed the document but also said it was nothing more than a pledge by the two countries to discuss ways to cooperate more closely on defence in the context of France's rapprochement with NATO.
"I believe it is a good thing," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Defence Ministry spokesman Alois Bach said it did not alter the United States' leading role in providing NATO's nuclear deterrent.

"This dialogue takes place on the basis of both countries' understanding that the most important nuclear guarantee for Europe and for NATO is the nuclear guarantee of the United States and none of that will change," Bach said.

Hausmann insisted there was nothing secret about the document, adding it was due to be published this week. Its release had been delayed merely to allow consultation with Germany's allies and the French and German parliaments, he said.
He said the document, which outlines a general concept for future Franco-German cooperation on defence issues, contained only one sentence on nuclear weapons.
"Our two countries are ready to begin a dialogue over the role of nuclear deterrence in the context of a European defence policy," Hausmann quoted the document as saying.
One foreign diplomat familiar with the text confirmed to Reuters that the nuclear element was only a small part of a larger document which contained no surprises.

Guenter Verheugen, deputy leader of the SPD in parliament, said he had not seen the document but added: "I consider the basic idea that the European Union develops a defence identity of its own and has its own instruments to be the right thing."

In Paris the French government agreed under left-wing opposition pressure to an emergency debate on the joint defence concept after protests that the document had been leaked to everyone except parliament.

After an international furore over French nuclear testing in 1995, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe called for discussion of a policy of "concerted deterrence" which implied Paris might consult its European allies over widening the definition of vital interests covered by its deterrent.
Germany renounced nuclear weapons after World War Two and accepted U.S. nuclear weapons on its soil during the Cold War as part of its NATO protection from the Warsaw pact.

According to extracts published in Le Monde, nothing in the document bars France from unilateral military actions but both countries agree "to consult about an intervention aimed at preventing or settling a crisis".

"All our conventional forces, including rapid reaction forces, are primarily at the service of the defence of our allies in the framework of obligations resulting from the Brussels and Washington treaties," it said, referring to the founding agreements of the Western European Union and NATO.
